reason: A gives the more credible causal analysis and study plan. Both identify several distinct problems and propose randomized rollout or difference-in-differences, but A more clearly specifies comparable controls, distinguishes modern staggered-adoption estimators from potentially biased two-way fixed effects, and tracks total outcomes alongside exposure-adjusted risk. That last distinction matters because reduced driving may itself be a benefit of bike lanes; B’s emphasis on per-trip or per-kilometre outcomes could miss part of the policy’s total effect. A also gives more concrete safeguards for regression to the mean, spillovers, and heterogeneous lane designs. Its illustrative event-study equation does not itself implement the recommended modern estimator, but overall its reasoning and design are stronger.
